topics.title: Bowel Elimination: How It Works and What Goes Wrong
topics.summary: Normal stool is soft, formed, brown, and about 75% water. When the bowel speeds up, slows down, or stops, you get diarrhea, constipation, or obstruction.
objectives: You can describe normal stool and how the bowel moves it along.
You can name the ten factors that change bowel elimination.
You can compare diarrhea, flatulence, constipation, and fecal incontinence and their risks.
You can tell diverticulosis from diverticulitis and name the three complications.
You can tell a mechanical obstruction from a paralytic ileus.
You can pick the first nursing action when obstruction or perforation is suspected.
topics.bigPicture:
Bowel elimination is how the body gets rid of solid waste. Waste is the part of food the body could not digest or absorb.

Picture the bowel as a conveyor belt running through a sponge. The belt carries waste along. The sponge, the colon wall, soaks up water. Speed is everything. Too fast, and stool comes out liquid (diarrhea). Too slow, and stool turns hard and dry (constipation). If the belt stops, the client has a bowel obstruction. That is an emergency. When you know the speed, you can predict the stool and the danger.
recap: Normal stool is about 75% water and 25% solids. It is soft, formed, and brown.
The colon absorbs water. Fast transit gives liquid stool; slow transit gives hard, dry stool.
Diarrhea risks fluid and electrolyte loss first, then skin breakdown. Older adults and infants dry out fastest.
Constipation is fewer than 3 BMs a week OR hard, dry stool that is hard to pass.
Liquid stool after days without a formed BM may be seepage around an impaction.
Fecal incontinence is usually a sign of another disorder. Look for the cause.
Diverticulitis means inflamed pouches. It can cause obstruction, perforation, or bleeding.
Mechanical obstruction is a physical block; paralytic ileus means the bowel stopped moving. Both risk necrosis and perforation.

keyTerms.def: Solid waste passed from the bowel. Normally about 75% water and 25% solid material.
The soupy mix of food and digestive juices that leaves the stomach.
Wave-like muscle squeezes that push contents forward through the digestive tract.
A strong wave of colon movement set off when food enters the stomach. It causes the urge to defecate after meals.
Two muscle rings at the anus. The internal one works automatically. The external one is under our control, so we can wait.
Gas passed from the bowel through the anus.
Passage of liquid feces with increased frequency.
Excessive gas in the intestines or colon.
Fewer than three bowel movements per week, or difficulty passing stools that may be hard and dry.
A mass of hard stool stuck in the rectum that the client cannot pass.
Inability to voluntarily control the passing of feces and intestinal gas through the anal sphincter.
Small pouches that bulge out of the colon wall where the lining pushes through weak spots. One pouch is a diverticulum.
Inflammation of the diverticula. It can cause obstruction, perforation, and bleeding.
A serious infection of the lining of the abdomen, often caused by bowel contents leaking in.
Inability of intestinal contents to move through the small or large bowel.
A functional obstruction. The bowel muscles become adynamic (stop moving), often after surgery or drugs such as anesthesia and opioids.
Necrosis is tissue death from lost blood flow. Perforation is a hole or tear that spills bowel contents into the abdomen.

sections.heading: How does the bowel make normal stool?
sections.keyIdea: The colon soaks up water, so the longer stool stays there, the harder it gets.
sections.body:
Food leaves the stomach as chyme, a soupy mix. The small intestine absorbs most nutrients. What is left moves into the large intestine (colon). The colon absorbs water and electrolytes and stores waste.

Peristalsis pushes stool along. When stool stretches the rectum, the person feels the urge to go. The internal sphincter works on its own. The external sphincter is under our control, so we can wait for a toilet.

Eating sets off the gastrocolic reflex. That is why many people feel the urge after a meal, often breakfast. You will use this reflex for bowel training.
bullets: Normal stool is about 75% water and 25% solid material.
The solids are bile, gut secretions, shed lining cells, bacteria, and minerals such as calcium and phosphate.
Small amounts of seeds, meat fiber, and fat are still normal.
Soft but formed: it holds a shape but is easy to pass. It needs normal fluid intake.
Brown comes from bile broken down by gut bacteria. Black, red, or clay-colored stool is a clue that something is wrong.
Gas: the bowel makes about 7–10 L of gas every 24 hours. Most is absorbed or moves along unnoticed.
sections.example: A client is worried about seeds in a soft, brown, formed stool. You reassure them. Small amounts of seeds or fiber are normal. Blood is not.

check.q: Why does stool get harder the longer it stays in the colon?
check.a: The colon keeps absorbing water from it. More time means more water removed, so the stool turns hard and dry.

sections.heading: What changes a person's bowel habits?
sections.keyIdea: When a bowel pattern changes, run through the ten factors to find the cause.
sections.body: Many things speed up or slow down the bowel. When a client's pattern changes, check each factor in this table. A post-op client often has several at once.

table.caption: Ten factors that affect bowel elimination
rows: Diet
Fiber adds bulk and holds water. Low fiber slows the bowel. Some foods cause gas or diarrhea.
Fluid
Too little fluid makes stool harder and drier.
Activity
Moving speeds up peristalsis. Bed rest slows it.
Defecation habits
Ignoring the urge lets stool dry out. No privacy or a new routine makes people hold it.
Medications
Opioids and iron constipate. Antibiotics can cause diarrhea. Laxatives speed the bowel.
Diagnostic procedures
Being NPO and bowel preps empty the bowel. Barium can harden afterward.
Anesthesia and surgery
Slow or briefly stop peristalsis.
Disease
Bowel disease or nerve damage, such as spinal cord injury, changes movement and control.
Pain
Hemorrhoids, an incision, or a perineal tear make the person put off a BM.
Stress and mood
Stress can speed the bowel and loosen stool. Depression can slow it.

check.q: A post-op client is on bed rest, takes opioids, and has been NPO. What bowel risk factors do you see?
check.a: At least four: low activity, opioids, low food and fluid intake, and anesthesia and surgery. All slow the bowel, so this client is at high risk for constipation.

sections.heading: Diarrhea: when the bowel moves too fast
sections.keyIdea: With diarrhea, protect fluid and electrolytes first, then protect the skin.
sections.body:
Diarrhea is liquid stool that comes more often than usual. Contents rush through too fast for the colon to absorb water. Water, sodium, and potassium leave with the stool.

Infants and older adults get dehydrated the fastest. So the first worry is fluid loss. Skin care comes next.
bullets: Hard-to-control urge: keep the call light, bedpan, or commode in reach. Answer calls fast.
Cramps and more frequent bowel sounds: the bowel is working hard and often.
Fluid and electrolyte loss: track intake and output and daily weights. Watch for dry mouth, low urine output, and dizziness on standing.
Skin breakdown: liquid stool carries enzymes and acids. Clean gently after each stool, pat dry, and apply a moisture barrier.
sections.example: An 82-year-old client has had six watery stools since morning. You check for dehydration and keep an accurate I&O. You protect the skin and keep the commode close. Then you report how often the stools come.

sections.heading: Flatulence: what causes too much gas?
sections.keyIdea: Gas comes from bacteria, swallowed air, the blood, certain foods, and slowed bowels after surgery.
sections.body: Flatulence means too much gas in the bowel. It causes bloating, cramping, and belching. There are five causes to know.
bullets: Bacteria acting on chyme: gut bacteria ferment food and give off gas.
Swallowed air: eating fast, chewing gum, straws, fizzy drinks, and fast anxious breathing.
Gas from the blood that moves into the bowel.
Gas-forming foods: beans, cabbage, onions, and cauliflower.
Abdominal surgery: peristalsis slows, so gas builds up. Walking as allowed is the best help.

sections.heading: Constipation: when the bowel moves too slow
sections.keyIdea: Constipation is fewer than three BMs a week OR hard, dry stool that is hard to pass.
sections.body:
Notice the word or. A client who goes every day but strains to pass hard stool is still constipated. Always compare with the client's own usual pattern.

The main cause is decreased motility. The bowel moves slowly, so the colon pulls out extra water. Constipation can be a problem by itself, from low fiber, low fluid, or inactivity. It can also be a sign of a hidden disorder, such as a nerve problem or a blockage. So a new or lasting change needs a closer look.

Hard stool can build into a fecal impaction. Then liquid stool may seep around the hard mass. It looks like diarrhea, but the real problem is a blockage.

check.q: A client has a BM every day but says, "I push really hard and it's like little rocks." Is this constipation?
check.a: Yes. Constipation is fewer than three BMs a week OR hard, dry stool that is hard to pass. A daily BM does not rule it out.

sections.heading: Fecal incontinence: why does control fail?
sections.keyIdea: Fecal incontinence is usually a sign of another disorder, so look for the cause.
sections.body:
Fecal incontinence means the client cannot control the passing of stool and gas. Control needs three things. The client must feel that the rectum is full. The sphincter must be strong. The brain must be able to respond. A problem with any one can cause leaking.

It is a symptom, not a disease. The nurse protects the skin and helps find the cause.
bullets: Nerve and brain disorders: stroke, spinal cord injury, and dementia.
Depression: it can lower the drive or ability to respond to the urge.
Injury: such as a sphincter tear during childbirth.
Inflammation or a mass in the bowel.
Hemorrhoids or a deformed anus that keeps the sphincter from closing.

check.q: Why is fecal incontinence called a "manifestation" rather than a disease?
check.a: Because it is usually a sign of another disorder, such as a nerve, injury, or inflammatory problem. The nurse protects the skin and helps find the cause.

sections.heading: Diverticulosis or diverticulitis: what's the difference?
sections.keyIdea: Diverticulosis means pouches are present; diverticulitis means the pouches are inflamed and can obstruct, perforate, or bleed.
sections.body:
In diverticular disease, the bowel lining pushes out through weak spots in the colon wall. This forms small pouches called diverticula. Just having the pouches is diverticulosis. Many people have no symptoms. Low fiber and straining are often linked to them.

Trouble starts when stool or bacteria get trapped and a pouch becomes inflamed. That is diverticulitis. Clients often have pain, commonly in the lower left belly. They may also have fever and changes in bowel habits.
bullets: Obstruction: swelling and scarring can narrow or block the colon.
Perforation: a pouch bursts and spills stool into the abdomen. This causes peritonitis. Watch for sudden worse pain, a rigid belly, and fever.
Bleeding: vessels near the pouches can bleed, so blood may pass from the rectum.
sections.analogy: Think of an old bike tire. Where the tire is thin, the inner tube bulges out in little bubbles. That is diverticulosis. If a bubble gets swollen and sore, it can block, burst, or bleed. That is diverticulitis.

check.q: A client with diverticulitis suddenly has much worse pain, a rigid abdomen, and fever. What do you suspect?
check.a: Perforation, which can cause peritonitis. Notify the provider immediately.

sections.heading: Bowel obstruction: when the bowel stops
sections.keyIdea: A blocked or stopped bowel swells, loses blood flow, and can die or tear, so report it fast.
sections.body:
A bowel obstruction means contents cannot move through the bowel. There are two kinds. The difference is why things stopped.

Bowel sounds give a clue. Early in a mechanical block, they are often high-pitched. With a paralytic ileus, they are hypoactive or absent.

table.caption: Two kinds of bowel obstruction
rows: Mechanical
Something physically blocks the bowel. The muscle may work hard, but contents can't get past.
Adhesions (scar bands, often after surgery); hernias (trapped bowel loop); intussusception (bowel telescopes into itself); volvulus (bowel twists); tumors
Functional
The bowel is open, but peristalsis has stopped. The motor quit.
Paralytic ileus. The muscles are adynamic (not moving), often after surgery or drugs such as anesthesia and opioids.

steps: Contents stop moving. Fluid, gas, and stool build up behind the block.
The bowel stretches. The client has distention, cramping pain, nausea and vomiting, and no stool or flatus.
Pressure in the swollen bowel squeezes its own blood vessels.
Without blood, the tissue dies (necrosis) and can tear (perforation). Fever, a fast heart rate, and a rigid belly are late warnings.
sections.example: Two days after abdominal surgery, a client's belly is distended and firm. The client feels sick and has passed no flatus. You hear no bowel sounds after listening for several minutes. This points to a paralytic ileus. Keep the client NPO as ordered and report it promptly. Expect an order such as a nasogastric tube.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Many bowel problems look alike at first, so look for the one clue that sets them apart.
sections.body: These pairs trip up students. Learn the clue that tells them apart.

table.caption: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
rows: Diarrhea vs seepage around an impaction
Seepage is small amounts of liquid stool after days with no formed BM. Assess for impaction before giving an antidiarrheal.
Daily BM vs "not constipated"
Hard, dry stool that is hard to pass is constipation, even if it happens every day.
Diverticulosis vs diverticulitis
-osis means the pouches are there. -itis means they are inflamed, with pain and fever.
Mechanical obstruction vs paralytic ileus
Mechanical: something blocks it; early bowel sounds often high-pitched. Ileus: the bowel stopped moving; sounds hypoactive or absent.
Fluid loss vs skin breakdown in diarrhea
Both matter, but fluid and electrolyte loss is the bigger threat. Treat it first.
Fecal incontinence as a disease vs a sign
It is usually a sign of another problem. Look for the cause, not just briefs.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect questions that ask you to spot obstruction or perforation and act before routine care.
sections.body: The NCLEX rarely asks for a definition alone. It gives you a client and asks what matters most. Watch for these patterns.
bullets: Priority: which client do you see first? A new rigid belly beats stable diarrhea.
Cue recognition: distention, vomiting, and no flatus after surgery suggest ileus.
Safe action: hold a laxative or antidiarrheal until you rule out obstruction or impaction.
Definitions in disguise: a client with daily hard stools, or the three diverticulitis complications.
steps: Read the stem: "A client is 2 days post-op. The abdomen is distended. No flatus. Bowel sounds absent. What is the nurse's first action?" Options: A) Give the ordered stool softener. B) Offer a warm drink. C) Keep NPO and notify the provider. D) Help the client walk.
What is it really asking? Can you spot a paralytic ileus and do the safe thing first?
Key cues: after surgery, distention, no flatus, absent bowel sounds.
Why the wrong options are wrong: A and B put more into a stopped bowel. D can help gas later, but it does not address a possible obstruction now.
The answer is C. Keep NPO as ordered and report, because ileus can lead to necrosis and perforation.
Reusable strategy: when the bowel may be blocked or stopped, put nothing in and get the provider involved.

sections.heading: Worked case: the quiet belly after surgery
sections.keyIdea: Connect the risk factors to the findings, then act on the danger, not the comfort need.
sections.body: Mr. Lee, 68, had colon surgery 2 days ago. He takes opioids for pain and has stayed in bed. Now he is nauseated and his belly is firm and swollen. He has not passed gas. He asks for something to help him "go."
steps: Spot the risks: surgery, anesthesia, opioids, and bed rest all slow the bowel.
Spot the cues: distention, nausea, no flatus. Listen in all four quadrants for several minutes.
Name the problem: this looks like a paralytic ileus, a functional obstruction.
Act safely: do not give a laxative. Keep him NPO as ordered and notify the provider.
Watch for worsening: fever, a fast heart rate, and a rigid belly can mean necrosis or perforation.

check.q: The next day Mr. Lee's belly becomes rigid and board-like and he has a fever. What changed, and what do you do?
check.a: These suggest necrosis or perforation, a complication of obstruction. Notify the provider immediately and stay with the client.

pearls: Speed sets the stool: too fast is liquid, too slow is hard, stopped is obstruction.
A daily BM does not rule out constipation. Ask about hard stool and straining.
With diarrhea, fluid and electrolytes come before skin care, especially in older adults.
Liquid stool after days without a BM? Think impaction before giving an antidiarrheal.
Early mechanical obstruction often has high-pitched bowel sounds. Paralytic ileus has hypoactive or absent sounds.
After abdominal surgery, walking as allowed helps move gas along.
redFlags: Distention, vomiting, cramping pain, and no stool or flatus: suspect obstruction. Keep NPO as ordered and report promptly.
Diverticulitis with sudden worse pain, a rigid board-like belly, and fever: possible perforation. Notify the provider immediately.
A hernia that turns firm and painful with vomiting: possible trapped bowel. Assess and report right away.
Many watery stools with dizziness, very low urine output, or confusion, especially in an infant or older adult: serious fluid loss. Report it.

checks.q: Why can diarrhea cause dehydration while constipation causes hard stool? Use what the colon does.
checks.a: The colon absorbs water. In diarrhea, contents move too fast to absorb water, so water is lost. In constipation, stool sits longer and more water is pulled out.

checks.q: Name three mechanical causes of obstruction and the main functional cause.
checks.a: Mechanical: any three of adhesions, hernias, intussusception, volvulus, and tumors. Functional: paralytic ileus.

checks.q: A client with diarrhea has red perianal skin and dizziness on standing. Which problem comes first?
checks.a: The dizziness. It suggests fluid loss. Check vital signs and fluid status and report. Then clean gently, pat dry, and apply a moisture barrier.

checks.q: A client who had no BM for 5 days now passes small amounts of liquid stool. An antidiarrheal is ordered as needed. What do you do first?
checks.a: Assess for fecal impaction before giving it. The liquid stool may be seeping around a mass of hard stool.

checks.q: A client with a stroke has new fecal incontinence. What is your approach?
checks.a: Treat it as a sign of the neurologic problem. Protect the skin, support toileting, and report it so the cause can be addressed.

topics.title: Bowel Assessment, Ostomies, and Diagnostic Tests
topics.summary: Bowel assessment starts with the client's story, then a stoma and abdominal exam where you listen before you touch, then knowing what each diagnostic test means for the client.
objectives: You can list what to ask in a bowel history, including elimination aids and ostomy care.
You can predict ostomy output from the stoma's location.
You can tell a healthy stoma from one that must be reported now.
You can do the abdominal exam in the right order and explain why.
You can describe what to observe in stool and what abnormal findings may mean.
You can give the key nursing points before and after common bowel tests.
topics.bigPicture:
Bowel habits are private, and many clients feel embarrassed. That makes your assessment skills even more important. A good bowel assessment answers three questions. What is normal for this person? What has changed? Why?

You gather answers three ways. You talk with the client (the history). You examine the abdomen, rectum, stool, and any ostomy. And you help with diagnostic tests that let the team see inside the bowel. Each step can catch bleeding, blockage, or fluid loss early.
recap: History: usual pattern, stool and changes, problems, elimination aids, diet, fluid, exercise, medications, stress, and any ostomy.
Ileostomy output is liquid and enzyme-rich. Colostomy output gets more formed the farther along the colon.
A healthy stoma is moist and pink to beefy red. Pale, dusky, purple, or black: report immediately.
Abdominal exam order: inspect, auscultate, percuss, palpate. Palpating first can change peristalsis.
Observe stool color, consistency, shape, amount, odor, and abnormal contents.
Black, tarry stool can mean upper GI bleeding, even in a client taking iron. Check vital signs and report.
After EGD: nothing by mouth, not even ice chips, until the gag reflex returns.
After barium: fluids and the ordered laxative. White stool for a day or two is expected.

keyTerms.def: A person's usual frequency, timing, and ease of bowel movements.
Anything a person uses to help have a BM, such as laxatives, enemas, suppositories, prune juice, or a morning coffee routine.
A surgically made opening from an inner organ to the body surface. A bowel ostomy lets stool leave through the abdominal wall.
The visible end of bowel brought out through the abdominal wall.
The skin right around the stoma.
An ostomy made from the colon (large intestine).
An ostomy made from the ileum, the last part of the small intestine.
Listening to body sounds with a stethoscope.
Sounds heard when tapping (percussing). Tympany is a drum-like sound over gas. Dullness can mean stool, fluid, or a mass.
Black, tarry stool that usually means bleeding high in the GI tract.
Blood in stool that is hidden (not visible) and found only by testing.
A drop in heart rate, sometimes with faintness, caused by stimulating the vagus nerve, as during rectal stimulation.
A flexible scope with a camera views the whole colon. Tissue samples can be taken and polyps removed.
Barium, a contrast liquid, is put into the colon through the rectum so x-rays can outline the bowel.
A scope passed through the mouth to view the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum.

mnemonics.name: Abdomen order: I-A-P-P
mnemonics.text: Inspect, Auscultate, Percuss, Palpate. Think "I Always Pause, Please": listen before you touch the belly.

sections.heading: What do you ask in a bowel history?
sections.keyIdea: Learn the client's own normal first, because a change from it is what matters.
sections.body:
Give privacy, use words the client knows, and stay matter-of-fact. Your comfort helps the client feel comfortable.

Normal frequency varies a lot, from several times a day to a few times a week. What matters most is the client's own usual pattern and any change from it.
bullets: Defecation pattern: "How often do you have a BM? What time of day?"
Stool and changes: "Any change in color, shape, or how hard or soft it is?"
Problems: diarrhea, constipation, gas, leaking, pain, or bleeding.
What affects it: elimination aids, diet, fluid, exercise, medications, and stress.
Ostomy: ileostomy or colostomy, how they care for it, and any skin, pouch, or coping problems.
sections.example: A client says, "I'm fine. I just take a laxative every night." That is a finding, not small talk. Daily laxatives can weaken the bowel's own reflexes. Ask how long they have used it and what happens without it.

sections.heading: Colostomy or ileostomy: what comes out?
sections.keyIdea: The farther along the bowel the stoma sits, the more water is absorbed and the more formed the stool.
sections.body:
An ostomy lets stool leave through the belly wall instead of the anus. The stoma is the end of bowel stitched to the skin. Stool collects in a pouch. Ostomies may follow cancer, obstruction, perforation, inflammatory bowel disease, or trauma. They can be temporary or permanent.

A colostomy comes from the colon. An ileostomy comes from the ileum. A stoma has no sphincter and no nerve endings for touch or pain. So the client can't control output and won't feel an injury.

table.caption: Stoma location and expected output
rows: Ileostomy
Liquid to pasty, drains often
Enzymes damage skin fast, so the pouch must fit well. High risk of dehydration and electrolyte loss. Track I&O.
Ascending colostomy
Liquid to semi-liquid
Like an ileostomy: protect skin and fluid balance.
Transverse colostomy
Mushy, semi-formed
Timing is unpredictable. A pouch is needed.
Descending colostomy
Semi-formed to formed
Closer to normal stool.
Sigmoid colostomy
Formed
Output may become regular enough to predict.

sections.analogy: Think of the colon as wringing out a wet towel. Cut in near the start, and the towel is still dripping. Cut in near the end, and it is nearly dry.

check.q: Who is at more risk for dehydration and skin breakdown: a client with an ileostomy or a sigmoid colostomy?
check.a: The ileostomy. Its output is liquid, frequent, and full of enzymes because it leaves before the colon can absorb water.

sections.heading: How do you assess a stoma?
sections.keyIdea: A healthy stoma is moist and pink to beefy red; a pale, dusky, purple, or black stoma is an emergency.
sections.body:
A healthy stoma looks like the inside of your mouth. It is moist, pink to beefy red, and usually sits a bit above the skin. It may bleed a little when cleaned. That is expected. After surgery it is swollen. The swelling goes down over weeks, so measure often and resize the pouch opening.

A stoma that is pale, dusky (bluish), purple, or black is not getting enough blood. The tissue can die. Report it to the surgeon immediately.
bullets: Peristomal skin: should be intact, with no redness, rash, or open areas.
Output: amount, color, consistency, and odor compared with what you expect for that location.
Fluid status: with an ileostomy, high output plus falling urine output, a fast pulse, or dizziness on standing needs follow-up first.
Pouch fit: any leaks, or an opening cut too large.
Coping and self-care: feelings about the body change, and ability to empty and change the pouch.
Delegation: assistive personnel (AP) may empty and measure an established pouch for a stable client. Stoma and skin assessment and teaching stay with the nurse.
sections.example: The morning after colostomy surgery, the stoma was moist and red. Now it is dark purple and dry. Blood flow has changed. Notify the surgeon right away and document what you see.

sections.heading: Why listen before you touch the abdomen?
sections.keyIdea: For the abdomen, auscultate before you palpate, because pressing can change bowel sounds.
sections.body: Most body systems use inspect, palpate, percuss, then auscultate. The abdomen is different. The order is inspect, auscultate, percuss, palpate. Pressing on the belly can alter peristalsis. It can stir up sounds or quiet them, which gives a false result.
steps: Inspect: shape (flat, rounded, distended), scars, movement, and skin. Distention plus past surgery should make you think of adhesions or ileus.

Auscultate: use the diaphragm in all four quadrants. Normal sounds are irregular clicks and gurgles, about 5–30 per minute. Note hypoactive, hyperactive, or absent. Listen for several minutes before you call them absent.
Percuss: tympany over gas is common. Dullness can mean stool, fluid, or a mass.
Palpate: light, then deep. Check for tenderness, firmness, or masses. Touch the painful area last.
Rectum and anus: inspect and palpate for hemorrhoids, fissures (small tears), skin breakdown, or leaking stool.
sections.analogy: It is like checking fish in a pond. You watch and listen first. If you throw a rock in first, you can't tell what was happening before.

check.q: Why does the nurse auscultate the abdomen before palpating it?
check.a: Palpation can alter peristalsis. That changes the bowel sounds and gives a false picture of bowel activity.

sections.heading: What do you look for in stool?
sections.keyIdea: Check six things in stool, and never assume black stool is just from iron.
sections.body: Observe six features: color, consistency, shape, amount, odor, and abnormal contents. Knowing the abnormal findings helps you catch problems early.

table.caption: Stool features
headers: Abnormal and what it may mean
rows: Color
Brown (infants: yellow to tan or green)
Black, tarry (melena): upper GI bleeding; iron can also darken stool. Red: low GI bleeding or beets. Clay or white: bile isn't reaching the bowel, unless barium was given recently.
Consistency
Soft, formed
Liquid (fast transit) or hard and dry (constipation).
Shape
Shaped like the rectum, about 2.5 cm across
Narrow, pencil-thin stool can mean something is narrowing the bowel, such as a mass.
Amount
Varies with diet
Small amounts of liquid stool with no formed stool may be seepage around an impaction.
Odor
Typical, affected by diet
Very foul odor can come from infection or blood.
Abnormal contents
Small amounts of seeds, fiber, or fat
Blood, pus, lots of mucus, parasites, greasy floating stool (fat), or swallowed objects.

sections.example: A client taking iron has dark, almost black stool. Iron can do this, but so can upper GI bleeding. Don't assume. Check vital signs, document it, and report it. If the pulse is fast or the blood pressure low, report it promptly.

sections.heading: Lab tests and the rectal exam
sections.keyIdea: Collect stool cleanly and send it fast, and watch for a slow heart rate during rectal stimulation.
sections.body: Some tests use blood or stool. Others need the provider to examine the rectum. Know what each looks for and your role.
bullets: Blood tests: a blood count looks for anemia from blood loss. Electrolytes check losses after diarrhea or vomiting.
Fecal tests: occult blood (hidden blood, used in colon cancer screening), stool culture (bacteria), and ova and parasites.
Collecting stool: use a clean container or a "hat" in the toilet. Keep out urine, toilet paper, and toilet water. Send it promptly. Follow any diet or drug rules for occult blood tests.
Digital rectal exam (DRE): the provider inserts a gloved, lubricated finger. It finds masses, hemorrhoids, hard stool, and, in men, an enlarged prostate.
During a DRE: place the client on their side and give privacy. Rectal stimulation can cause a vagal response. If the heart rate drops or the client feels faint, stop the stimulation first.

sections.heading: Scope and x-ray tests: before and after
sections.keyIdea: Know the prep before each test and the one danger sign to watch for after it.
sections.body: These tests let the team see inside the bowel. EGD looks at the upper GI tract. Colonoscopy looks at the colon. Don't mix them up.

table.caption: Bowel tests and nursing points
rows: Colonoscopy
A scope views the whole colon. Biopsies can be taken and polyps removed.

Before: consent; clear liquids and a laxative prep until output is clear liquid. After: vital signs as sedation wears off; gas and cramps are expected. Report severe pain, a distended or rigid belly, fever, or heavy bleeding.
Barium enema
Barium goes into the colon through the rectum, then x-rays outline the bowel.
Before: the bowel must be empty. After: push fluids and give the ordered laxative, because barium can harden. White or chalky stool for a day or two is expected.
Colorectal transit study
The client swallows a capsule with markers. X-rays over several days show how fast they move.
Used for constipation and slow bowels. The client usually avoids laxatives and enemas so results show true speed.
EGD
A scope through the mouth views the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum.
Before: NPO and consent. The throat is numbed. After: nothing by mouth, not even ice chips, until the gag reflex returns. Report severe pain or bleeding.

check.q: A client back from an EGD asks for water. What must you check first?
check.a: That the gag reflex has returned. The throat was numbed, so drinking too soon could cause aspiration.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Expected findings and danger signs can look alike, so compare against what this client should have.
sections.body: These look-alikes cause wrong answers. Learn the clue that sets them apart.

table.caption: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
rows: Beefy red stoma vs dusky stoma
Moist, beefy red is healthy. Pale, dusky, purple, or black means poor blood flow. Report now.
Liquid ileostomy output vs fluid loss
Liquid output is expected. A fast pulse, dizziness, or low urine output is not.
Black stool from iron vs melena
Iron stool is dark but usually not tarry. Melena is black, sticky, and tarry. Don't assume. Check vital signs and report so the stool can be tested.
White stool after barium vs clay-colored stool
White for a day or two after barium is expected. Clay stool without barium means bile isn't reaching the bowel.
Gas after colonoscopy vs perforation
Gas and cramps are expected. Severe pain, a rigid belly, or fever is not.
Colonoscopy prep "liquid" vs "clear"
Prep is done when output is clear liquid, not just liquid.
EGD vs colonoscopy
EGD is upper GI through the mouth. Colonoscopy is the colon through the rectum.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect questions that make you pick the danger sign out of several expected findings.
sections.body: Many items list several normal findings and one dangerous one. Your job is to find the one that does not fit.
bullets: Exam order: what does the nurse do right after inspecting the abdomen?
Stoma findings: which stoma color needs immediate report?
Post-test priorities: after EGD, colonoscopy, or barium, which finding or teaching is correct?
Stool findings: which stool change needs follow-up?
steps: Read the stem: "A client had a colonoscopy 2 hours ago. Which finding should the nurse report?" Options: A) Passing gas. B) Mild cramping. C) A rigid abdomen with fever. D) Feeling drowsy.
What is it really asking? Which finding is not an expected effect of the test?
Key cues: recent scope through the colon; "rigid" and "fever" together.
Why the wrong options are wrong: A and B come from air put in during the test. D is expected as sedation wears off.
The answer is C. A rigid belly with fever suggests perforation. Notify the provider immediately.
Reusable strategy: sort each option into "expected after this procedure" or "not expected." Report the one that is not expected.

sections.heading: Worked case: a new ileostomy
sections.keyIdea: With an ileostomy, fluid loss outranks skin, pouch, and body-image concerns.
sections.body: Ms. Ortiz, 45, had an ileostomy 3 days ago. Her pouch fills with liquid stool many times a day. She is drinking less because she feels sick. Today her pulse is 112, she feels dizzy standing up, and her urine is dark and scant. The skin near the stoma is red, and she cries when she looks at it.
steps: What is expected? Liquid output is normal for an ileostomy.
What is not? A fast pulse, dizziness on standing, and low, dark urine signal fluid volume loss.
Rank the problems: fluid loss is the priority. Red skin and grief are real but less urgent.
Act: check vital signs and I&O and notify the provider. Check the stoma color too.
Then: refit the pouch to protect the skin, and listen to her feelings before teaching.

check.q: Which finding in Ms. Ortiz would also need an immediate call to the surgeon?
check.a: A stoma that turns pale, dusky, purple, or black. That means poor blood flow, and the tissue can die.

pearls: Abdomen: inspect, auscultate, percuss, palpate. Light before deep, and the painful area last.
Listen in all four quadrants for several minutes before you document absent bowel sounds.
Ileostomy and ascending colostomy: liquid. Sigmoid colostomy: formed.
Treat routine laxative use as a cue. Ask how long and what happens without it.
Colonoscopy prep is complete when output is clear liquid, not just liquid.
During a transit study, no laxatives or enemas, so results show the bowel's true speed.
redFlags: A stoma that turns pale, dusky, purple, or black: poor blood flow. Notify the surgeon immediately.
Black, tarry stool with dizziness, a fast heart rate, or low blood pressure: possible GI bleeding. Check vital signs and report promptly.
After colonoscopy, severe pain, a distended or rigid belly, fever, or heavy rectal bleeding: possible perforation. Notify the provider immediately.
High ileostomy output with falling intake and urine output: fluid loss. Report it before it becomes severe.
Slow heart rate and faintness during rectal stimulation: vagal response. Stop the stimulation first.

checks.q: A client has an ascending colostomy. Will you expect formed or liquid stool? Why?
checks.a: Liquid to semi-liquid. The stoma is early in the colon, so little water has been absorbed yet.

checks.q: List the six stool features to observe.
checks.a: Color, consistency, shape, amount, odor, and abnormal contents.

checks.q: A client had a barium enema yesterday and has not had a BM. Why is this a concern, and what do you do?
checks.a: Barium can harden and cause constipation or impaction. Push fluids, give the ordered laxative, and report if the barium is not passed.

checks.q: A client has clay-colored stool and has had no recent barium test. What may this mean?
checks.a: Bile may not be reaching the bowel. Document and report it.

checks.q: Can you delegate emptying a stable client's established ostomy pouch to AP? What stays with you?
checks.a: Yes, AP may empty and measure it. The nurse keeps stoma and skin assessment and all teaching.

topics.title: Bowel Care, Prevention, and Risk Factors
topics.summary: Most bowel care is nursing care: fluid, fiber, teaching, bowel training, exercises, hygiene, and ostomy care. Medications and surgery are added when needed, and prevention depends on asking directly.
objectives: You can tell independent nursing measures from collaborative therapies.
You can teach fluid, fiber, and food choices safely.
You can set up a bowel training routine that uses the gastrocolic reflex.
You can teach basic ostomy care and support the client's feelings.
You can compare laxatives, stool softeners, and antidiarrheals and know when to hold them.
You can teach prevention, name modifiable risks, and screen with direct questions.
topics.bigPicture:
Bowel care comes in two groups. Independent interventions are things a nurse can start without an order. These include fluid and fiber, teaching, bowel training, pelvic floor exercises, hygiene, and ostomy care. Collaborative therapies need the team. These are medications and surgery.

Start with the independent measures. They fix the cause, while drugs often treat only the symptom. A client who drinks enough, eats fiber, moves, and answers the urge may never need a laxative. The best care of all is prevention, and most prevention is teaching.
recap: Independent: fluid and fiber, diet teaching, bowel training, Kegels, hygiene, ostomy care. Collaborative: medications and surgery.
Raise fiber slowly and with fluid. Check for a fluid restriction first.
Schedule bowel training after a meal, usually breakfast, upright, with privacy and time.
Never give a laxative when obstruction is suspected. Hold it and notify the provider.
Long-term laxative use weakens the bowel's natural reflexes.
Empty an ostomy pouch at one-third to one-half full. Cut the barrier to fit closely.
Incontinence and retention are never normal. There is no standard screening, so ask directly.

keyTerms.def: An action a nurse can start without a provider's order, based on nursing judgment.
Treatment that needs a provider's order or the team, such as medications or surgery.
The part of plant foods the body can't digest. It adds bulk and holds water in stool.
A program that sets a regular time and routine for BMs to restore a predictable pattern.
Tightening and relaxing the pelvic floor muscles again and again to strengthen bowel and bladder control.
A cream or ointment that shields skin from stool and urine.
The sticky wafer that attaches the pouch to the skin and protects the skin around the stoma.
A medication that promotes a BM by adding bulk, drawing water into the bowel, or stimulating peristalsis.
A medication that lets water mix into stool so it passes without straining.
A medication that slows bowel movement to reduce diarrhea.
A risk the person can change or reduce, such as obesity or diet. Age and family history are not modifiable.
A nurse specialist who helps with stoma fitting, skin problems, and ostomy teaching.

sections.heading: Why start with fluid and fiber?
sections.keyIdea: Fiber holds water in stool, so fiber only works when the client drinks enough fluid.
sections.body:
The first independent step is more fluid and fiber. They work as a team. Fiber adds bulk and holds water, which keeps stool soft. The bulk stretches the bowel wall and triggers peristalsis. Fluid gives the fiber water to hold. Fiber without fluid can make stool harder and cause bloating.

Teach clients how food choices change their bowel. Help them make small swaps they can keep.
bullets: Fiber sources: whole grains, fresh fruit, vegetables, beans, and bran. Goals are about 25 g a day for women and 38 g for men.
Go slow: raise fiber gradually to limit gas and bloating.
Fluid: unless restricted, encourage about 2,000 mL or more a day, spread out.
Check first: a client with heart failure or kidney disease may have a fluid limit. Follow orders.
Foods that constipate: low-fiber processed foods and large amounts of cheese and meat.
Foods that loosen stool: fruit (especially prunes), vegetables, and whole grains.
Gas-formers: beans, cabbage, onions, cauliflower, and fizzy drinks.
Irritants: caffeine, alcohol, artificial sweeteners, and spicy or acidic foods.
sections.example: A client with constipation eats white rice and chicken every night and drinks coffee all day. You suggest brown rice, a vegetable at dinner, fruit for snacks, and water in place of some coffee.

check.q: Why should a client raise fluid at the same time as fiber?
check.a: Fiber works by holding water in stool. Without enough fluid, extra fiber can make stool harder and cause bloating.

sections.heading: How does bowel training work?
sections.keyIdea: Bowel training uses the same time each day, right after a meal, to teach the bowel a schedule.
sections.body: Bowel training sets a regular time for BMs. It helps clients with chronic constipation, fecal incontinence, or nerve problems. It works because the bowel responds to routine and to the gastrocolic reflex after eating.
steps: Learn the client's usual pattern. Pick a set time, ideally after a meal, often breakfast.
Offer a warm drink with or after the meal. Warm fluids can help stir the bowel.
Help the client onto the toilet or commode. Sit upright, feet supported, leaning slightly forward. Use a bedpan only if nothing else works.
Give privacy and enough time. Don't rush.
Teach the client never to ignore the urge.
Repeat at the same time daily, with fluid, fiber, and activity. A pattern may take weeks.
sections.analogy: It is like a body clock. Go to bed at the same time every night, and you get sleepy on schedule. Sit on the toilet after breakfast each day, and the bowel learns too.
bullets: Delegation: AP can carry out the toileting schedule. The nurse teaches, assesses, and evaluates the program.

sections.heading: Pelvic floor exercises and hygiene
sections.keyIdea: Kegels strengthen bowel and bladder control, and gentle cleaning after every stool protects the skin.
sections.body:
Kegel exercises strengthen the muscles that support the rectum and bladder, including the anal sphincter. They help both fecal and urinary incontinence. The client tightens the muscles used to hold back stool or stop urine. They hold a few seconds, relax, and repeat several times a day.

Personal hygiene protects the skin and stops infection from spreading.
bullets: Clean the perineal area gently after every stool and pat it dry.
Wipe front to back to keep stool bacteria away from the urethra.
Apply a moisture barrier when skin is often exposed to stool.
Wash hands after toileting and before handling food. This is the key to stopping infectious diarrhea from spreading.

sections.heading: What does good ostomy care include?
sections.keyIdea: A close-fitting barrier and a pouch emptied at one-third to one-half full prevent leaks and skin damage.
sections.body:
Ostomy care is an independent nursing measure. Much of it is teaching the client to manage at home. Leaking stool damages skin quickly, so fit matters most.

Many clients grieve the change in their body. When a client is upset, acknowledge the feeling and invite them to talk before you teach.
bullets: Empty the pouch at about one-third to one-half full. A heavy pouch can pull loose.
Change the skin barrier on schedule, or sooner if it leaks.
Measure the stoma. Cut the opening only slightly larger than the stoma, so skin is covered but the stoma isn't squeezed.
Clean the skin with warm water, pat dry, and inspect the stoma and skin each change.
Teach how to empty and change the pouch and which foods cause gas or odor. With an ileostomy, teach the client to drink enough to replace losses.
Get help: involve the wound and ostomy nurse.
sections.example: A client with a new ileostomy says the skin burns and the pouch keeps leaking. You find the barrier opening cut far larger than the stoma. Enzyme-rich stool is on the skin. You re-measure, cut it to fit closely, protect the skin, and ask the wound and ostomy nurse to follow up.

sections.heading: Bowel medications: when to give, when to hold
sections.keyIdea: Never give a laxative when obstruction is suspected, and check with the provider before an antidiarrheal if infection is possible.
sections.body: When nursing measures aren't enough, the provider may order medications. Surgery is used for obstruction, ulceration, perforation, or cancer. It may remove part of the bowel and sometimes creates an ostomy.

table.caption: Bowel medications
rows: Laxatives (bulk-forming psyllium; osmotic polyethylene glycol [Miralax]; stimulant bisacodyl or senna)
Promote a BM by adding bulk, drawing water into the bowel, or stimulating peristalsis

Never give with suspected obstruction or unexplained belly pain. Give bulk-formers with a full glass of water and keep fluids up. Long-term use weakens natural reflexes and can cause dependence and electrolyte loss.
Stool softeners (docusate)
Let water mix into stool so it passes without straining

For clients who shouldn't strain: after surgery or childbirth, with hemorrhoids, or on opioids. They prevent hard stool over time. They are not for quick results. For opioid constipation, a softener alone is usually not enough, so a stimulant such as senna is usually added.
Antidiarrheals (loperamide)
Slow the bowel so more water is absorbed
Check with the provider if infection is possible, such as with fever or blood. Slowing the bowel can keep the germ or toxin inside. Watch for constipation and bloating. Keep replacing fluids.

check.q: A client with distention, vomiting, and no flatus asks for a laxative. What do you do?
check.a: Hold it and notify the provider. These are signs of possible obstruction. A laxative raises pressure behind the block and the risk of perforation.

sections.heading: How does bowel health link to other concepts?
sections.keyIdea: Problems in thinking, fluids, infection, inflammation, mobility, or teaching can all cause bowel problems.
sections.body: Bowel elimination links to six other concepts. Trouble in any of them can cause bowel problems. Bowel problems can cause trouble in them too.

table.caption: Related concepts
rows: Cognition
A client with dementia may not notice the urge or find the bathroom. New agitation can be a sign of constipation, so check for a physical cause before giving a sedative.
Fluids and electrolytes
Diarrhea drains fluid and electrolytes. Low fluid intake causes hard stool.
Infection
Infections cause diarrhea. Stool on skin or near the urethra spreads infection.
Inflammation
An inflamed bowel, as in diverticulitis, can obstruct or perforate.
Mobility
Immobility slows peristalsis and makes it hard to reach the toilet in time.
Teaching and learning
Diet, fluids, routines, and ostomy care all depend on good teaching.

sections.heading: Prevention and risks the client can change
sections.keyIdea: Many of the same habits protect both bladder and bowel, and many risk factors can be changed.
sections.body: Prevention covers both bladder and bowel. Teach habits the client can keep. Then target the risks they can change.
bullets: Keep a healthy weight and exercise regularly. Extra weight presses on the pelvic floor; activity moves the bowel.
Don't delay voiding or defecation. Held stool dries out, and the urge weakens.
Don't use the pelvic floor muscles to force urine out. Straining weakens them.
Eat a high-fiber diet with enough fluid.
Treat constipation or diarrhea early, before impaction, dehydration, or skin breakdown.
Don't smoke. Smoking is a risk for urinary and fecal incontinence, and chronic cough strains the pelvic floor.
Avoid irritants such as caffeine, alcohol, artificial sweeteners, and spicy or acidic foods.

table.caption: Modifiable risk factors
rows: Obesity
Extra belly weight presses on the bladder and pelvic floor.
Pregnancy
The uterus presses on the bowel and bladder, and hormones slow the bowel. Birth can injure the pelvic floor.
Procedures needing anesthesia
Anesthesia slows peristalsis and can cause constipation or ileus.
Drugs for other conditions
Opioids and iron constipate. Antibiotics can cause diarrhea.
Lower income and less education
Less access to healthy food, health information, and care.
Poor hygiene
Germs spread from stool to mouth and cause infectious diarrhea.
Poor diet; poor cooking and storing of food
Low fiber causes constipation. Undercooked or poorly stored food causes foodborne illness.
Travel, especially to developing countries
Unsafe water and food cause traveler's diarrhea. Teach bottled or treated water and well-cooked food.

sections.heading: Screening: why you have to ask
sections.keyIdea: No standard screening exists, so ask directly and kindly, because clients rarely bring it up.
sections.body:
There are no standard screening tests for elimination problems. Instead, nurses and providers ask about symptoms at regular checkups, especially with older adults.

These problems need more direct questions than most. Clients feel embarrassed or think leaking is part of aging. But urinary incontinence and retention are never normal. They often point to another medical problem. The same is true of fecal incontinence.
sections.example: Instead of "Any problems?", you say: "Many people have trouble with leaking urine or stool, or with constipation. Do you ever leak when you cough or can't reach the bathroom in time? How often do you have a BM?" Direct, normalizing questions get honest answers.

check.q: An 80-year-old says, "I leak a little urine, but that's normal at my age." How do you respond?
check.a: Explain that incontinence is never normal and often points to a treatable problem. Report it so the provider can evaluate it.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: The safest answer often means holding a drug or checking first, not doing more.
sections.body: These pairs look similar but lead to different actions.

table.caption: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
rows: Push fluids vs fluid restriction
Push fluids only after you check for a restriction, such as heart failure or kidney disease.
Laxative for constipation vs suspected obstruction
Distention, vomiting, and no flatus mean hold the laxative and call.
Stool softener vs quick relief
Softeners prevent straining over time. They don't give fast results or treat opioid constipation alone.
Antidiarrheal for any diarrhea vs infectious diarrhea
Fever or blood? Check with the provider first.
Independent vs collaborative
Fluid, fiber, training, Kegels, hygiene, and ostomy care are independent. Drugs and surgery are collaborative.
Modifiable vs non-modifiable
Obesity, diet, smoking, and drugs can change. Age and family history cannot.
Teaching a grieving client vs listening
Acknowledge feelings first. Teaching sticks better after.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect items where the right action is to hold, check, or teach rather than give a drug.
sections.body: The NCLEX tests whether you know when a bowel drug is safe. It also tests whether your teaching is correct.
bullets: Hold or give: a PRN laxative for a client who may have an obstruction.
Best teaching: which statement shows the client understands fiber, bowel training, or ostomy care?
Delegation: what can AP do in a bowel program?
Prevention: which risk factor can the client change?
steps: Read the stem: "A client on opioids after surgery has had no BM in 3 days. The belly is soft, bowel sounds are present, and flatus is passing. Docusate is ordered. What should the nurse do?" Options: A) Keep giving docusate alone and recheck in 3 days. B) Ask the provider about adding a stimulant laxative such as senna. C) Hold all bowel medications. D) Limit fluids.
What is it really asking? Do you know a softener alone is usually not enough for opioid constipation?
Key cues: opioids and no BM, but no signs of obstruction.
Why the wrong options are wrong: A waits while the problem grows. C is for suspected obstruction, which is not present. D makes stool harder.
The answer is B. Collaborate to add a stimulant, since there are no signs of obstruction.
Reusable strategy: before any bowel drug, ask two things. Is there a sign of obstruction? Does this drug match the cause?

sections.heading: Worked case: building a bowel program
sections.keyIdea: Combine fluid, fiber, timing, position, and teaching, and avoid relying on daily laxatives.
sections.body: Mr. Banks, 70, lives in a rehab unit after a stroke. He has hard stools every 4 days and some leaking. He drinks little because he fears accidents. He has no fluid restriction.
steps: Find the causes: low fluid, low activity, and a nerve problem from the stroke.
Fluid and fiber: offer fluids regularly through the day. Add fiber slowly.
Timing: set toileting shortly after breakfast to use the gastrocolic reflex.
Position and privacy: commode or toilet, upright, feet supported, leaning forward, no rushing.
Delegate and evaluate: AP follows the schedule. You assess stool, skin, and progress, and teach Mr. Banks and his family.

check.q: Mr. Banks asks for a laxative every night "to be safe." What do you teach?
check.a: Routine laxative use weakens the bowel's own reflexes. Fluid, fiber, activity, and the after-breakfast routine work better long term. Report his request to the provider.

pearls: Always check for a fluid restriction before pushing fluids, and increase fiber gradually.
Give bulk-forming laxatives with a full glass of water.
For opioid constipation, collaborate to add a stimulant laxative when there are no signs of obstruction.
Peristomal skin damage with leaks usually means a poor fit. Re-measure and cut the opening to fit closely.
Watch clients on antidiarrheals for constipation. Report it when stool stops and bloating starts.
Screen with direct, normalizing questions that name specific symptoms.
redFlags: A client asking for a laxative who has distention, vomiting, and no stool or flatus: hold it and notify the provider.
Diarrhea with fever or blood, or that continues after an antidiarrheal: report it. Infection may need different treatment.
Raw or open peristomal skin: stool is leaking onto skin. Refit the pouch and involve the wound and ostomy nurse.
New agitation in a client with dementia: check for constipation or another physical cause before a sedative.

checks.q: Which two independent measures come first for constipation, and how do they work together?
checks.a: Fluid and fiber. Fiber adds bulk and holds water. Fluid supplies the water, so stool stays soft and keeps moving.

checks.q: When is the best time for bowel training, and why?
checks.a: After a meal, often breakfast. Eating triggers the gastrocolic reflex, which pushes stool toward the rectum.

checks.q: A postpartum client fears a painful first BM. What helps?
checks.a: A stool softener as ordered, plus fluids and fiber. Never advise her to delay the BM.

checks.q: A traveler is going to a developing country. What bowel teaching applies?
checks.a: Travel is a risk for diarrhea. Drink bottled or treated water, eat well-cooked food, and wash hands.

checks.q: Which is a modifiable risk factor: age, family history, or obesity?
checks.a: Obesity. Age and family history cannot be changed.

topics.title: Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
topics.summary: Normal bowel elimination changes with age, from seedy yellow baby stools to toilet training, slow bowels in pregnancy, and constipation in older adults.
objectives: You can describe normal newborn and infant stools and how feeding changes them.
You can state the expected ages for bowel control and toilet training.
You can recognize intussusception and act on it as an emergency.
You can explain bowel changes during pregnancy and after birth.
You can explain why older adults get constipated and why laxative overuse backfires.
You can decide when a change in bowel habits must be referred.
topics.bigPicture:
The same stool can be normal in one client and worrying in another. A loose, mustard-yellow, seedy stool is normal for a breastfed baby. In an adult, it would be diarrhea. A child not toilet trained at 2 is on track. At 5, the child may need evaluation.

This lesson walks through each stage of life: newborns and infants, toddlers, school-age children and teens, pregnancy, and older adults. For each one, learn what is normal, what is common, and what should make you act.
recap: Most newborns pass meconium within 24 hours. Report none by about 48 hours.
Breastfed stool is mustard yellow and seedy. Formula-fed stool is tan to yellow to green, often pasty.
Infant stool gets firmer and smells stronger once solid foods start.
Some bowel control at 18–24 months. Toilet training is usually done by 36–48 months.
Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction under age 3. Notify the provider immediately.
Pregnancy: progesterone slows the bowel and the growing uterus presses on it. Hemorrhoids come late.
Older adults: constipation is common. Laxative overuse can make it worse.
A change in bowel habits lasting weeks, blood in stool, or new fecal incontinence needs referral.

keyTerms.def: A newborn's first stools: thick, sticky, and greenish-black.
Lighter stools that come after meconium in the first days, before normal infant stools.
The soft spot on a baby's head. A sunken fontanel is a sign of dehydration.
A wave of colon activity set off when food enters the stomach. It often causes the urge to defecate after a meal.
Learning to control bowel and bladder and use the toilet. It is usually done by 36–48 months.
One part of the intestine slides (telescopes) into the next, blocking it. The most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children under 3.
Stool mixed with blood and mucus that looks like red jelly. A sign of intussusception, usually a later one.
A pregnancy hormone that relaxes smooth muscle, including the muscle of the GI tract.
Swollen veins in the rectum or anus, made worse by pressure and straining.

sections.heading: What are a newborn's first stools?
sections.keyIdea: Most newborns pass meconium within 24 hours; report a newborn with no stool by about 48 hours.
sections.body:
A newborn's first stools are meconium. They are thick, sticky, and greenish-black. Most newborns pass meconium within the first 24 hours. No stool by about 48 hours should be reported. It can signal a blockage or another problem.

Over the next few days, stools turn lighter. These are transitional stools. Then normal infant stools appear. How often a baby stools varies and depends on breast or formula feeding. Breastfed babies often stool more, sometimes after every feeding.

check.q: A newborn is 50 hours old and has passed no stool. What should the nurse do?
check.a: Report it. Most newborns pass meconium within 24 hours. None by about 48 hours can signal a blockage or another problem.

sections.heading: Breastfed or formula-fed: what's normal?
sections.keyIdea: Loose, seedy, mustard-yellow stool is normal for a breastfed baby, and tan to green is normal with formula.
sections.body: Parents often worry about the color and looseness of baby stool. Use this table to reassure them. Then teach what would be worrying.

table.caption: Infant stools
rows: Color
Mustard yellow
Tan to yellow to green
Look
Seedy (small curds)
Less seedy, more pasty
Consistency
Soft and liquid
Soft and liquid, often a bit pastier
Odor
Faint
Faint, but usually stronger

bullets: Stool gets firmer when the infant starts solid food.
Odor stays faint until solids, then smells more like adult stool.
Switching from breast milk to formula can change how stool looks.
Worrying signs: very watery stools far more often than usual, or blood. Also watch for dehydration: fewer wet diapers, a dry mouth, or a sunken fontanel.
sections.example: A new mother says, "My breastfed baby's diaper is full of runny yellow stuff with little seeds. Is it diarrhea?" You reassure her that this is normal. Then you teach the warning signs of dehydration to watch for.

check.q: A formula-fed infant has a green, pasty stool. Is this abnormal?
check.a: No. Formula-fed stools normally range from tan to yellow to green and are often pasty.

sections.heading: When do toddlers gain bowel control?
sections.keyIdea: Expect some control at 18–24 months and full toilet training by 36–48 months, started when the child is ready.
sections.body:
Bowel control depends on nerves and muscles that mature with age. Two ages matter.

Start toilet training when the child shows readiness signs, not by a set date or a sibling's timeline.
bullets: Some bowel control: 1.5 to 2 years (18–24 months).
Successful toilet training: 36 to 48 months (3 to 4 years).
steps: Watch for readiness: the child can walk to the toilet, sit, pull pants down, stay dry a couple of hours, show interest, and say they need to go.
Use a routine: sit on the potty after meals to use the gastrocolic reflex.
Praise success. Never punish accidents. Pressure can make a child hold stool, which causes constipation.
Expect setbacks during stress, such as a new sibling, a move, or illness.
sections.analogy: Toilet training is like learning to ride a bike. The child needs balance and strength before practice works. There will be some falls along the way.

sections.heading: Intussusception: why is it an emergency?
sections.keyIdea: Waves of severe pain with knees to chest, vomiting, and currant jelly stool in a young child mean intussusception.
sections.body: Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children under 3. One section of bowel slides inside the next, like a telescope folding in. This is a mechanical obstruction. Stool can't pass, and the folded bowel's blood supply gets squeezed. Without treatment, the tissue can die and perforate.
bullets: Sudden, severe, crampy pain in waves. The child screams and draws the knees to the chest.
Calm or sleepy between episodes.
Vomiting.
Currant jelly stool: blood and mucus. This is usually a later sign.
Sometimes a sausage-shaped lump in the abdomen.
sections.analogy: Picture rolling a sock down so it folds inside itself. The rolled part gets thick and tight. The tight fold pinches off the blood supply.
sections.example: A parent brings in a 10-month-old who keeps screaming and pulling his legs up. He vomited twice. Now there is red, jelly-like stool in the diaper. You notify the provider immediately. This needs prompt diagnosis and treatment.

check.q: What is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children under 3?
check.a: Intussusception, when one part of the intestine telescopes into the next.

sections.heading: School-age children and teens
sections.keyIdea: Children who hold stool, often to avoid school bathrooms, become constipated.
sections.body:
By school age, bowel habits are similar to adults'. Frequency, amount, and consistency vary from child to child.

Adult risk factors start to show up. Busy days and embarrassment about school bathrooms can lead children to hold stool. Held stool dries out and gets hard. Fast food with few fruits, vegetables, and little water adds to it. Teach fiber, water, activity, and never ignoring the urge.

check.q: A 9-year-old has hard stools and never uses the school bathroom. What is the link?
check.a: Holding stool lets it dry out and harden, causing constipation. Teach not to ignore the urge, plus fiber, water, and activity.

sections.heading: How does pregnancy change the bowel?
sections.keyIdea: Progesterone slows the bowel and the growing uterus presses on it, so constipation and bloating are common.
sections.body: Pregnancy slows the bowel in a predictable chain. After birth, new problems appear. Manage constipation with fluid, fiber, and activity. The client should not stop prescribed prenatal vitamins without talking to the provider.
steps: High progesterone relaxes smooth muscle, including the GI tract.
This causes delayed stomach emptying and less peristalsis.
Slower movement lets the colon absorb more water. This may cause bloating and constipation.
The growing uterus presses on the bowel and makes it worse. Iron in prenatal vitamins can add to it.
Late in pregnancy, pressure on rectal veins plus straining leads to hemorrhoids.
bullets: Sluggish bowels after birth: labor, less food, and stretched belly muscles slow things down.
Pain delays elimination: a sore perineum, stitches, or hemorrhoids make her afraid to go. Delay hardens stool and makes the next BM worse.
Gas after cesarean birth: surgery and anesthesia slow peristalsis. Early, frequent walking helps most.
sections.example: On day 1 after birth, a client with a perineal tear is afraid to have a BM. You give pain medicine as ordered and the stool softener if ordered. You encourage fluids, fiber, and walking. You explain that soft stool makes the first BM less painful. You never advise her to wait.

sections.heading: Why are older adults often constipated?
sections.keyIdea: Low activity, low fluid and fiber, weak muscles, and medications slow the bowel, and laxative overuse makes it worse.
sections.body: Constipation is common in older adults. Four causes explain most of it. Many older adults also believe they need a BM every day. Teach that normal varies, and every day is not required.

table.caption: Why older adults get constipated
rows: Less activity
Less movement slows peristalsis.
Encourage walking as tolerated.
Low fluid and fiber
Less thirst, limiting fluids to avoid accidents, dental problems, less fresh food.
Offer fluids regularly. Suggest soft high-fiber foods like cooked vegetables, oatmeal, and prunes.
Muscle weakness
Weaker belly and pelvic muscles make pushing harder.
Use an upright, supported position. Encourage activity.
Medication side effects
Many drugs, such as opioids and iron, slow the bowel.
Review the list and report drugs that may contribute.

bullets: Respond to the gastrocolic reflex: help the client to the toilet after meals, especially breakfast. Answer call lights fast, or the urge may be lost.
Laxatives can backfire: routine use weakens natural reflexes. The bowel depends on the drug, the client takes more, and the cycle continues.
EDUCATE: teach fluid, fiber, activity, and routine instead of daily laxatives. Report laxative use rather than raising the dose.

check.q: An older adult takes a stimulant laxative every night and says it works less well now. What is happening?
check.a: Routine use weakens the bowel's natural reflexes, so constipation can get worse. Teach natural measures and report the laxative use to the provider.

sections.heading: When is a bowel change a warning sign?
sections.keyIdea: A change in an older adult's bowel habits lasting weeks must be referred, never written off as aging.
sections.body:
A change in bowel habits over weeks should be referred to the primary care provider. Examples are new constipation, new diarrhea, thinner stools, or blood in the stool. These can be early signs of a serious problem such as colorectal cancer. Its risk rises with age.

Fecal incontinence is not a normal part of aging either. It usually signals another problem that can often be treated. Refer it for evaluation, rather than just supplying briefs.
sections.example: A 74-year-old says her stools have been thinner for a month. She also has constipation that switches with loose stools. She shrugs it off as age. You urge her to see her primary care provider soon, and you document and report it.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: What is normal depends on age, so always ask what is normal for this client's stage of life.
sections.body: These look-alikes come up often. Learn the clue that tells them apart.

table.caption: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
rows: Loose breastfed stool vs infant diarrhea
Seedy yellow is normal. Watery stools far more often, with fewer wet diapers or a sunken fontanel, are not.
Green formula stool vs illness
Tan to yellow to green is normal for formula.
Fussy baby vs intussusception
Intussusception has waves of severe pain with knees to chest, calm between, vomiting, and currant jelly stool.
Toilet training by age vs by readiness
Start when the child shows readiness signs, not by a date or a sibling's timeline.
Pregnancy constipation vs stopping vitamins
Use fluid, fiber, and activity. Don't stop prenatal vitamins without the provider.
"Just aging" vs a warning sign
A change lasting weeks, blood, or new incontinence needs referral.
Chronic change vs acute obstruction
Distention, vomiting, and no flatus are urgent. They outrank slow, chronic changes in an older adult.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect age-norm questions and priority questions where one child or client has an emergency.
sections.body: Lifespan items often ask what is normal for an age. Others ask which call or client needs you first.
bullets: Age norms: breastfed vs formula stool, meconium timing, toilet training ages.
Priority: which child's symptoms suggest intussusception?
Teaching: postpartum and pregnancy bowel care; older adults and laxatives.
Referral: which older adult's change needs the provider?
steps: Read the stem: "The nurse returns phone calls. Which call is first?" A) A breastfed 2-week-old with seedy yellow stools. B) A 2-year-old with screaming spells, knees drawn up, and vomiting. C) A formula-fed infant with green stool. D) A 3-year-old not yet toilet trained.
What is it really asking? Which child has an emergency, and which are normal?
Key cues: under 3, waves of pain, knees to chest, vomiting.
Why the wrong options are wrong: A and C are normal stools. D is still within the 36–48 month range.
The answer is B. These signs suggest intussusception. Call back first and send the child for prompt care.
Reusable strategy: rule out the options that are normal for that age. The one left is usually the priority.

sections.heading: Worked case: an older adult and laxatives
sections.keyIdea: Teach natural measures, report laxative overuse, and refer lasting changes.
sections.body: Mrs. Price, 79, takes a laxative every night. She says, "I must go every day, but it isn't working anymore." She drinks little, walks little, and takes iron. For 6 weeks her stools have been narrower.
steps: Find the causes: low fluid, low activity, iron, and nightly laxatives.
Explain the cycle: routine laxatives weaken natural reflexes and can worsen constipation.
Correct the belief: a BM every day is not required. Normal varies.
Teach: fluids through the day, soft high-fiber foods, walking, and toileting after breakfast.
Refer: narrower stools for 6 weeks is a lasting change. Report it to the provider.

check.q: Mrs. Price asks to double her laxative dose. What is your best response?
check.a: Do not raise the dose. Explain that more laxative can worsen the problem, teach natural measures, and report her laxative use and stool change to the provider.

pearls: Breastfed stool: mustard yellow and seedy. Formula stool: tan to yellow to green, often pasty.
Know the age norms: meconium usually within 24 hours (report none by 48), control at 18–24 months, training by 36–48 months.
Intussusception: severe pain in waves, knees to chest, calm between, vomiting, currant jelly stool.
After a cesarean, early and frequent walking is the best relief for gas pain.
Older adults: answer the urge promptly, especially after breakfast. A delayed urge may be lost.
Fecal incontinence is never a normal part of aging. Refer it.
redFlags: A young child with screaming spells, knees to chest, vomiting, and red jelly-like stool: suspect intussusception. Notify the provider immediately.
A newborn who hasn't passed meconium by about 48 hours: report it. It may mean a blockage.
An infant with watery stools far more often than usual, fewer wet diapers, or a sunken fontanel: dehydration. Report it.
An older adult with a bowel change lasting weeks, blood in stool, or new incontinence: refer to the provider.

checks.q: Why is constipation common in pregnancy? Give two reasons.
checks.a: Progesterone delays stomach emptying and slows peristalsis. The growing uterus presses on the bowel and makes it worse.

checks.q: A mother says her 6-month-old's stools got firmer and smellier after starting cereal and pureed vegetables. Is this expected?
checks.a: Yes. Infant stool becomes firmer and smells stronger once solid foods start.

checks.q: Why might a postpartum client become constipated even if she was regular before?
checks.a: Bowels are sluggish after birth. Pain from a tear, stitches, or hemorrhoids can make her delay, which hardens stool.

checks.q: Which action best uses the gastrocolic reflex for an older adult with constipation?
checks.a: Help the client to the toilet shortly after meals, especially breakfast, and answer the urge promptly.

checks.q: A parent wants to start toilet training at 15 months because a cousin trained early. What do you teach?
checks.a: Start when the child shows readiness signs, not by a date or another child's timeline. Some control comes at 18–24 months.
